Do the following using the steps provided in their respective sections.
        Steps:
        1. clone the repo git@github.com:zelarhq/nodejs-welcome.git
        2. analyse the contents of the repo and create following.
            2.1 create/update dockerfile based on the analysis. 
            2.2 kubernetes yamls based on the analysis.
            2.3 github actions file to build application on pushing to main branch.
        3. add all changed file to git changes 
        4. commit / push to repo

function.name: create_a_docker_file
function.description: This function generates a Dockerfile in the specified directory with basic configuration. The Dockerfile will be tailored to a simple Python application. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Dockerfile will be created. It should be a valid directory path relative to the current working directory.

base_image.description: The base image to use for the Dockerfile, representing the starting point for the build.

maintainer.description: The name of the maintainer or author of the Dockerfile.

expose_port.description: The port number that the container should expose. This is typically the port that the application listens on.

entrypoint.description: The command that will be executed when the Docker container starts.

function.name: create_kubernetes_yaml_file
function.description: Generates a Kubernetes deployment and service YAML file in the specified repository directory. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Kubernetes YAML file will be created. This should be the root directory of the repository.

deployment_name.description: The name of the deployment to be created. This should be a unique identifier for the deployment.

image_name.description: The name of the Docker image to be used in the deployment. Include the image version tag if necessary.

replicas.description: The number of replicated pods desired in the deployment.

port.description: The port number that the container exposes for communication.

service_type.description: The type of Kubernetes service to be created for the deployment.

message.content:
I’m happy to walk you through what you’d normally do, but I don’t have the ability to actually clone a repo, touch files on your machine, or push commits back to GitHub from here.  
Below is a step‑by‑step guide you can copy‑paste into a terminal (or adapt to your own workflow). I’ll also show you the exact contents of the files you’ll want to create/modify so you can verify them before committing.

---

## 1️⃣ Clone the repository

```bash
git clone git@github.com:zelarhq/nodejs-welcome.git
cd nodejs-welcome
```

> **Tip** – If you’re using HTTPS instead of SSH, replace the URL with `https://github.com/zelarhq/nodejs-welcome.git`.

---

## 2️⃣ Analyse the repo & create the artefacts

### 2.1 Create / update the Dockerfile

Assuming the repo contains a simple Node.js app that listens on port `3000` (the common default for Express apps), a minimal Dockerfile would look like this:

```dockerfile
# Dockerfile
FROM node:18-alpine

# Set the working directory inside the container
WORKDIR /usr/src/app

# Copy package.json and package-lock.json first to leverage Docker cache
COPY package*.json ./

# Install dependencies
RUN npm ci --only=production

# Copy the rest of the source code
COPY . .

# Expose the port the app listens on
EXPOSE 3000

# Start the application
CMD ["npm", "start"]
```

If the repo already has a Dockerfile, compare it with the snippet above and adjust as needed.  
If you prefer to let me generate the file for you, you can call the helper function:

```python
from functions import create_a_docker_file

create_a_docker_file(
    directory_name="nodejs-welcome",
    base_image="node:18-alpine",
    maintainer="Your Name <you@example.com>",
    expose_port=3000,
    entrypoint='["npm","start"]'
)
```

> **Note** – The function will write a `Dockerfile` in the specified directory. You’ll still need to review it manually.

### 2.2 Generate Kubernetes YAML

A typical deployment for a Node.js app might expose port `3000` and use a `ClusterIP` service. Here’s a ready‑to‑use YAML:

```yaml
# k8s/deployment.yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome-deployment
spec:
  replicas: 3
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: nodejs-welcome
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: nodejs-welcome
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: nodejs-welcome
        image: zelarhq/nodejs-welcome:latest   # Replace with your registry/tag
        ports:
        - containerPort: 3000
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome-service
spec:
  type: ClusterIP
  selector:
    app: nodejs-welcome
  ports:
  - protocol: TCP
    port: 80          # Service port
    targetPort: 3000  # Container port
```

If you’d like the helper function to generate a similar file:

```python
from functions import create_kubernetes_yaml_file

create_kubernetes_yaml_file(
    directory_name="nodejs-welcome",
    deployment_name="nodejs-welcome-deployment",
    image_name="zelarhq/nodejs-welcome:latest",
    replicas=3,
    port=3000,
    service_type="ClusterIP"
)
```

> **Tip** – Store the YAML under a `k8s/` folder (or whatever you prefer) and commit it.

### 2.3 Create a GitHub Actions workflow

Create a file at `.github/workflows/build.yml` with the following content:

```yaml
name: Build & Push Docker Image

on:
  push:
    branches:
      - main

jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest

    steps:
      - name: Checkout source
        uses: actions/checkout@v4

      - name: Set up Docker Buildx
        uses: docker/setup-buildx-action@v3

      - name: Log in to Docker Hub
        uses: docker/login-action@v3
        with:
          username: ${{ secrets.DOCKERHUB_USERNAME }}
          password: ${{ secrets.DOCKERHUB_TOKEN }}

      - name: Build and push image
        uses: docker/build-push-action@v5
        with:
          context: .
          file: ./Dockerfile
          push: true
          tags: zelarhq/nodejs-welcome:latest
```

> **Important** – Add two secrets to your GitHub repo (`Settings → Secrets → Actions`):
> * `DOCKERHUB_USERNAME`
> * `DOCKERHUB_TOKEN` (a Docker Hub personal access token)

---

## 3️⃣ Stage the new/updated files

```bash
git add Dockerfile k8s/deployment.yaml .github/workflows/build.yml
```

> If you used the helper functions, they already wrote the files; just stage them.

---

## 4️⃣ Commit & push

```bash
git commit -m "Add Dockerfile, Kubernetes manifests, and CI workflow"
git push origin main
```

> After pushing, the GitHub Actions workflow will automatically trigger on the next push to `main`.

---

### Quick sanity check

Run the following locally to make sure everything builds:

```bash
# Build the Docker image
docker build -t zelarhq/nodejs-welcome:latest .

# Run the container
docker run -p 3000:3000 zelarhq/nodejs-welcome:latest
```

Open `http://localhost:3000` and confirm the app responds as expected.

---

## Recap

| Step | What you do |
|------|-------------|
| 1 | `git clone … && cd …` |
| 2.1 | Write or generate a Dockerfile (see snippet or helper) |
| 2.2 | Write or generate Kubernetes YAML (see snippet or helper) |
| 2.3 | Create `.github/workflows/build.yml` (see snippet) |
| 3 | `git add …` |
| 4 | `git commit … && git push` |

Feel free to copy the snippets above into your editor, tweak them to match your exact repo layout, and then run the commands. Once you’ve verified the files locally, commit and push them to GitHub. That’s all you need to get the CI/CD pipeline running!
